chapter: Failure in St. Louis and the Omaha bands
title: Nat Towles band: Buddy Tate, Henry Coker, C. Q. Price, Bob Dorsey
summary: Buddy Tate taught Thompson much; Henry Coker, C. Q. Price and Bob Dorsey were in the band, and Dorsey replaced Tate when Tate joined Basie; Debo Mills drummed.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: So that your arrangements carried that flavor. Well, now Nat Towles' band, Buddy Tate was in that band, wasn't he?
Yes, Buddy Tate was the main featured soloist in that band.
Yes.

He was a very good solo player, and Buddy had had much experience, and he was a very, very nice person, and a lot of personality. And the fact of the matter is Buddy Tate was very instrumental in helping me learn a lot of the things that I learned about music, and of course we had a very warm friendship because he liked to play and practice, and I was always willing to practice and play with him. And we learned a lot from eachother.
That's wonderful.
Yes.
Who else was in the band, Nat Towles' band. There were a number of musicians who made a success in New York afterwards, weren't there?
Well, there was some. Henry Coker later on --
Yes, went with Basie.
-- became a member of Count Basie's orchestra. He was a very, very wonderful trumpet -- trombone
player, still is. And in fact he was one of the most excellent trombone players I've ever heard in my life, and still is -- I consider him to be one of the greatest trombone players in the world.
And there was also a saxophonist by the name of Charles Price, known as C. Q. Price.
Oh, yes.
He was quite an arranger, and saxophonist. He later went with Count Basie, after having played a little while with Horace Henderson's band.
Right.
And there was another very good friend of mine named Bob Dorsey who was also in that band. He took Buddy Tate's place when Buddy Tate joined Count Basie.
Right.

It was during that time, in the late thirties, '38 or '39, somewhere around there, that Count Basie had a misfortune with one of his famous saxophonists. Herschel Evans died, and he called Buddy Tate to take his place.
Yes.
So we had to have someone to take Buddy's place, and it was this friend of mine, Robert Dorsey, who was a very excellent saxophonist.
And who did he go to afterwards?
He joined Horace Henderson's band along

with some of the other musicians around Omaha; the drummer's name was Debo Mills who I played with with Lloyd Hunter who was a great jazz drummer. and he was with some other musicians. I can't remember all of their names.
How do you spell Debo?
D-e-b-o. Isn't that odd? Debo Mills. M-i-i-l-l-s.
Oh, yes, right.
He was a great drummer, a great drummer, great drummer.
